title: A home kirtan
hookLine: invite friends to sing a shabad at home
tomorrow: Jas wants Simran on a video kirtan. does a screen count as sangat?

lines: A HARMONIUM OUT OF THE CLOSET.
cards: Friday night, living room, the coffee table pushed against the wall. Harjit has dragged his old harmonium out of the closet and is wiping dust off the keys. Bebe sits on the sofa with her gutka.
Maya sits cross-legged on a cushion, a scarf over her hair because Simran said she could borrow one. Before they start, Maya asks the question Simran asked yesterday. Why sing it?

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS SET IN RAAG.
teach.b: Sikhs give an answer from the page itself. Open the Guru Granth Sahib and its hymns are arranged by raag, the musical mode it's meant to be sung in. The Gurus wrote songs.
On Ang 1075 Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: in this dark age, kirtan, singing the Lord's praise, is foremost. Reading takes in the words.

Singing slows them down, gives them a tune the heart can hum on a Tuesday, and lets a room breathe the same line together. A home kirtan is just that: a few people, a shabad, maybe a harmonium, maybe only clapping.
Maya listens to the first verse, then laughs softly. My grandma does this at the stove, she says. Hymns, every morning.

Her grandma's Bible has a line for it, in Colossians, in the King James words: "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."
There's the shared thing: two families who sing the holy words at home so the words live in the house. And the honest difference.
Kirtan sings Gurbani itself, the Guru's own words, in the raag written at the top of the hymn. Maya's grandma's hymnbook holds psalms alongside songs written by later believers.
Two kitchens, two songbooks, one habit of singing the holy words where people live.

how: Sikh families hold kirtan at home for blessings, birthdays and ordinary evenings: a shabad or two sung with harmonium and tabla or simple clapping, often closing with Ardas and karah prashad.

o: friends and family singing a shabad together at home
a recorded kirtan played on a speaker in the car
a concert by professional singers at a gurdwara

games.q: two homes, two songbooks — tap the pairs.
p: the musical mode a hymn is set in
in this age, kirtan is foremost
psalms and hymns and spiritual songs
singing Gurbani, the Guru's own words

s: kirtan is only for trained musicians in a gurdwara hall
a home kirtan is a few people and a shabad, with a harmonium or just clapping.
the Guru Granth Sahib arranges its hymns by raag
the Gurus wrote songs; each hymn names the raag it is sung in.
Maya's grandma's hymns and kirtan are the same thing with different names
both sing holy words at home; kirtan sings Gurbani itself, her hymnbook adds songs by later believers.

games.q: a friend from a church family says, 'we sing hymns at home too, so it's basically the same as your kirtan.' what's the fairest reply?
o: we share the habit of singing holy words at home; kirtan sings Gurbani itself.
it's exactly the same, every religion is just singing to God.
no, kirtan is a much older and more serious kind of music.
games.why: the honest version names the shared habit and the real difference, and ranks neither: two songbooks, one habit.

practice: Play one shabad you know, quietly, or hum a single line of any song you hold sacred. Listen to that one sound the whole sit: where the tune rises, where it rests.
If you don't have one, listen to the hum of your own breath going out, long and low, and let that be the note.

wordCard.voice: A home kirtan. Friends and family singing a shabad together in the living room, with a harmonium or just clapping.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirtan, singing the praise of God, in Sikh life the singing of Gurbani.

carryVoice: Your line for today: kirtan at home, so the words live where you live. Day 1714, sung.
